title: The Innocent Cluster
text:
Thus, as if playing, I brought my heart near you

Long ago, in a spring...

But you, indifferent, passed by my side...

Long ago.


Wise in all things, perhaps you did not know

That girl's game that discreetly covered

With innocent laughter the tremendous secret,

Wise in all things...


Today, returned to my side, already a woman, you ask me

For that heart that in silence was yours,

And with clumsy negative words I argue

Today, returned to my side.


Oh, when I offered you my heart in that

Spring, the heart was a sweet untouched cluster...

Already others have tasted the grapes

Of the innocent cluster...
editorial_note: The translation keeps the grape-cluster metaphor and the repeated temporal returns.

title: Two Words
text:
Tonight in my ear you told me two words

common. Two words tired

of being said. Words

that from old are new.


Two words so sweet that the moon that was

filtering through the branches

stopped at my mouth. So sweet two words

that an ant walks along my neck and I do not try

to move to cast it off.


So sweet two words

that I say without wanting to —oh, how beautiful, life!—

So sweet and so gentle

that fragrant oils spill over the body.


So sweet and so beautiful

that nervous, my fingers,

move toward the sky imitating scissors.

Oh, my fingers would like

to cut stars.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the ordinary words becoming physically radiant.

title: Song of the Astute Woman
text:
Every rhythmic moon that passes I am called,

by God's grave numbers, to give my life

into another life: a mixture dyed blue ink;

the same strange mixture with which it has been kneaded.


And through my flesh, miserable and tired,

filters a warm wind of promised land,

and my dilated nose drinks, sweet aroma,

the exultant forest and the nourished branch.


A deceptive siren song you sing to me,

cunning nature! You attract and enchant me

so as to load me later with some human fruit.


Deceit for deceit: my beauty slips away

from the solemn call; from this living fever,

some sterile and passing love enjoys.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the poem's negotiation with fertility, nature, and chosen sterility.

title: Seven Lives
text:
I have seven lives, I have seven lives.

Seven lives of gold; lovely and florid.

Head cut off, head replaced:

My tree-spirit sprouts again in the siesta.


Purple dragon of flowering claws,

seven lives I have, I have seven lives.

Giants and dwarfs: cut off my heads,

they will grow stubborn as weeds.


I have seven lives, I have seven lives,

seven lives of gold lovely and florid

that irons tire and swords notch,

yet one day they will be forever felled.


The prince I await will dry

the seven flowering heads. Without

abracadabras,

the winged dragon will lose its lives

beneath the slender edge of

sweet words.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the fairytale dragon refrain and the paradox of defeat by sweet words.

title: It Could Be
text:
It could be that everything I have felt in verse

was nothing more than what could never be,

nothing more than something forbidden and repressed

from family to family, from woman to woman.


They say that in the ancestral houses of my people, measured

was everything that had to be done...

They say the women were silent

in my maternal house... Ah, it could well be...


At times in my mother cravings emerged

to free herself, but there rose to her eyes

a deep bitterness, and in the shadow she wept.


And all this biting, conquered, mutilated,

all this that was locked inside her soul,

I think that without wishing it I have set free.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the generational feminist argument direct and legible.

title: Seven Lives
text:
To Mrs. María A. S. de Fontán


I have, I have seven lives.

of gold;

lovely and florid.

Head cut off, head replaced:

My tree-spirit

sprouts again in the siesta.


Purple dragon of flowering claws,

seven lives I have, I have seven

lives.

Giants and dwarfs: cut off my heads,

they will grow stubborn as

the weeds.


I have, I have seven lives,

seven lives of gold lovely and

florid


that irons tire and swords notch,

yet one day they will be forever

felled.


The prince I await will dry

the seven flowering heads. Without

abracadabras,

the winged dragon will lose its lives

beneath the slender edge of

sweet words.
editorial_note: This layout-damaged version preserves the dedication and fractured lineation from the source.

title: Finished Journey
text:
What are your eyes, long from looking at me, doing?

What is your tongue, long from calling me, doing?

What are your hands, long from stretching

toward my flames, doing?


What is your long shadow doing behind my shadow?

Why do you prowl around my house?

In yesterday's kiss I made my journey.

I know your soul.


For what more? I have finished the journey.

Your catacombs flooded with waters

dead, dark, swampy, were

felt by my hands.


Let your hands not even come near mine,

turn away from me your eyes, your words...

the molds of your baseboards dried

the roots of my plants.


I hate your long eyes.

I hate your long hands.

I hate your catacombs

full of water.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the repeated longness and the decisive refusal after the completed journey.

title: Aymé!
text:
And you knew how to love, and you were prudent,

and it was spring and you were good,

and the sky was blue, resplendent.


And you kissed my hands with sweetness,

and looked into my eyes with your eyes,

which sometimes bit with bitterness.


And I passed by like ice itself...

I passed by without seeing where I was

neither the cruel hell nor the kindly sky.


I felt nothing... In the void

I wandered with the soul condemned

to my satanic and somber pain.


And I let you go silently,

you, who knew how to love and were good,

and were sweet, magnanimous and prudent.


Every pleading word was too little for you,

but pain closed my ears...

Ah, the soul was like hard rock.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the repeated goodness of the beloved against the speaker's numbness.

title: I Am Going to Sleep
text:
Teeth of flowers, bonnet of dew,

hands of grasses, you, fine nurse,

have ready for me the earthy sheets

and the comforter of weeded mosses.


I am going to sleep, my nurse, lay me down.

Put a lamp at my headboard;

a constellation; whichever you like;

all are good; lower it a little.


Leave me alone: you hear the buds breaking...

a celestial foot rocks you from above

and a bird traces some measures for you


so that you forget... Thank you. Ah, one errand:

if he calls again by telephone

tell him not to insist, that I have gone out...
editorial_note: The translation keeps the lullaby plainness and the famous final telephone instruction.

title: Thus
text:
I made the book like this:

Moaning, weeping, dreaming, ah me.


Sad butterfly, cruel lioness,

I gave lights and shadow all at once.

When I was lioness I never remembered

How one day I could have been butterfly.

When butterfly I never thought

That one day I could set sail or bite.


Shrunken at times and then by leaps

They bled my life and I killed with blood.

Whether now dove, heavy cypress.

Or flowering thicket, I wept and wept more.

Now tasting salts, now tasting honey,

The eyes wept beyond their strength.

Then it matters the same, for I have seen it well,

To be rose or thorn, to be nectar or gall.


Thus I go by curves with my bad thirst

Pruning gardens of every sort.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the shifting self-figures of butterfly, lioness, dove, cypress, rose, and thorn.
